paragraphs.heading: Order on the inside
paragraphs.text: A crystal is a solid whose building blocks, such as atoms, molecules or ions, sit in a highly ordered microscopic structure. That structure forms a crystal lattice extending in all directions. The scientific definition rests on this arrangement of atoms inside, called the crystal structure: in a crystal, the atoms form a periodic arrangement. The study of crystals and how they form is known as crystallography.

paragraphs.heading: Three kinds of solid
paragraphs.text: Snowflakes, diamonds and table salt are examples of large crystals. Most inorganic solids, though, are polycrystals: many microscopic crystals fused into one solid. Most metals, rocks, ceramics and ice are like this. In a block of ice, each small crystal, called a crystallite or grain, is a true crystal, but the pattern is broken at the grain boundaries, so the block as a whole has no periodic arrangement. A third kind, the amorphous solid, has no periodic structure at all; glass, wax and many plastics are examples. Despite its name, lead crystal is a type of glass and not a crystal.

paragraphs.heading: The unit cell
paragraphs.text: A crystal structure is described by its unit cell, a small imaginary box holding one or more atoms in a specific arrangement in space. Unit cells are stacked in three dimensions to make the crystal. They have to stack perfectly, with no gaps, and this requirement limits the symmetry a crystal can have. There are 219 possible crystal symmetries, called crystallographic space groups, and they are grouped into 7 crystal systems. In the cubic system crystals may form cubes or rectangular boxes, as halite does; in the hexagonal system they may form hexagons, as ordinary water ice does.

paragraphs.heading: Shape is a clue, not the definition
paragraphs.text: People commonly recognise crystals by their shape: flat faces with sharp angles. That shape is not required. A crystal is defined by its microscopic atomic arrangement and not by how it looks from outside, though the characteristic shape is often present and easy to see. Crystals with obvious, well-formed flat faces are called euhedral. Those without are called anhedral, usually because the crystal is one grain inside a polycrystalline solid.

paragraphs.heading: Why the faces are flat
paragraphs.text: Some surface orientations are more stable than others. While a crystal is growing, fresh atoms stick readily to the rough, less stable patches of its surface and less readily to the flat, stable ones. The flat surfaces therefore tend to grow larger and smoother, until the whole surface of the crystal is made of them.

paragraphs.heading: One substance, more than one shape
paragraphs.text: Take galena as an example. Its crystals often take the shape of cubes, and sometimes they form octahedrons. The six faces of the cube and the eight faces of the octahedron reflect different symmetries of the same crystal system, the isometric system. A crystal's visible outer shape is called its habit. Habit is set by the crystal structure, by the specific chemistry and bonding of the crystal, and by the conditions under which it formed.

paragraphs.heading: Crystals underfoot
paragraphs.text: The greatest concentrations of crystals in the Earth, whether counted by volume or by weight, are part of its solid bedrock. Crystals found in rocks are typically between a fraction of a millimetre and several centimetres across. Exceptionally large ones are occasionally found.
